SOURCE: Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS / Meta Agent Search), Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Jeff Clune; ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2408.08435v2, 2 Mar 2025).
COVERAGE: 34 of 34 pages; all 117,811 chars extracted. Main text, Tables 1-6, appendices A-J read in full. The reference list and the Appendix G agent code listings were only skimmed, and part of the Appendix F/G text was cut off in my view of it.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Defining agents as code and having a meta agent program new ones from an archive of past discoveries beats hand-designed agents in every domain tested.
  number: DROP 79.4 F1 vs best hand-designed 65.8 (Role Assignment); MGSM 53.4% vs 39.0% (LLM Debate); MMLU 69.6 vs 65.9; GPQA 34.6 vs 31.6.
  setup: Search run independently per domain, 30 iterations. Meta agent GPT-4 (gpt-4o-2024-05-13). Discovered agents and baselines run on gpt-3.5-turbo-0125. Held-out test sets, 95% bootstrap CI. Validation 128 questions, test 800 (GPQA diamond: 32 validation, 166 test, 5 evals).
  quote: "Meta Agent Search (Ours) 79.4 ± 0.8 53 .4 ± 3.5 69 .6 ± 3.2 34 .6 ± 3.2"
  where: Table 1, p7
- The gain is large on reading and math and small on multi-task and science. The authors hypothesise the cause: knowledge-limited tasks gain less from better agent structure. This is stated as a hypothesis, not tested.
  number: "improvements in F1 scores by 13.6/100 and accuracy rates by 14.4%"
  setup: as above
  quote: "We hypothesize that for challenging questions in the Science and Multi-task domains, the knowledge in FMs is not sufficient to solve the questions, limiting the improvement through optimizing agentic systems"
  where: Sec 4.2, p7
- On MMLU and GPQA the margins over the strongest baselines are inside the CIs (MMLU 69.6 ± 3.2 vs OPRO 67.6 ± 3.2; GPQA 34.6 vs Self-Refine 31.6, both ± 3.2). This is my reading of Table 1, not a statement in the paper.
  quote: "Prompt Optimization (Yang et al., 2024) 69.1 ± 0.9 30 .6 ± 3.2 67.6 ± 3.2 32 .9 ± 3.2"
  where: Table 1, p7
- The code search space beats prompt-only optimisation (OPRO) in all four domains.
  number: DROP 79.4 vs 69.1; MGSM 53.4 vs 30.6
  quote: "Meta Agent Search consistently outperforms them across all domains."
  where: p7
- ARC case study: the search progressed through "stepping stones", and the best agent combined three earlier ideas.
  number: 25 iterations; stepping stones at iterations 3, 5, 11, 12; best agent roughly 13-14% on ARC with GPT-3.5.
  setup: ARC "Public Training Set (Easy)" with grids ≤5×5; 20 validation and 60 test questions, each evaluated 5 times; meta agent GPT-4; agents on GPT-3.5.
  quote: "the ideas of incorporating diverse feedback, evaluating for various specific traits (via experts) such as efficiency and simplicity, and simulating human-like feedback emerged in iterations 5, 11, and 12, respectively."
  where: Sec 4.1, p6; Fig 3, p5
- Transfer within math: agents searched on MGSM beat baselines on held-out math sets.
  number: GSM8K 69.5 vs 43.6 (best baseline LLM Debate), +25.9 points; GSM-Hard 31.2 vs 18.0 (Role Assignment), +13.2 points.
  setup: top 3 MGSM agents moved to other tasks, GPT-3.5, test accuracy with 95% CI.
  quote: "our agents improve accuracy by 25.9% on GSM8K and 13.2% on GSM-Hard compared to the baselines when transferring within math domains."
  where: Sec 4.3, p8; Table 2
- Transfer beyond math is mixed. Reading comprehension: 70.4-71.9 F1 vs 65.8. MMLU: 62.4-67.0 vs 65.9, so one of the three agents scores below the best baseline. GPQA: 28.6-29.9 vs 31.6, a match at best.
  quote: "they still outperform (in Reading Comprehension and Multi-task) or match (in Science) the state-of-the-art hand-designed agent baselines."
  where: App A, Table 5, p20
  note: the text claims outperform on Multi-task, but "Dynamic Role-Playing Architecture" scores 62.4 ± 3.4 on MMLU against Role Assignment 64.5 and COT-SC 65.9. Treat the authors' wording as generous.
- Transfer across models on ARC: agents searched with GPT-3.5 keep their lead on stronger models.
  number: Dynamic Memory and Refinement Agent 12.7 (GPT-3.5), 9.7 (Haiku), 37.0 (GPT-4), 48.3% (Claude-Sonnet). Best baseline on Sonnet is Self-Refine at 39.3.
  quote: "Dynamic Memory and Refinement Agent† 12.7 ± 3.9 9.7 ± 3.3 37 .0 ± 5.3 48 .3 ± 5.7"
  where: Table 3, p9
  note: GPT-4 here is gpt-4o-2024-05-13. The agent chosen as best on GPT-3.5 was not the top agent on the other models. Another discovered agent was best on GPT-4/Sonnet, and Structured Feedback and Ensemble scored 5.0 on Haiku, near the bottom of the table. Self-Refine on Sonnet (39.3) roughly ties two of the three discovered agents.
- Starting from an empty archive still beats hand-designed baselines. Seeding with human baselines helps in three of four domains. In math, empty initialisation was better.
  number: Math 67.5 (empty) vs 53.4 (seeded); DROP 73.9 vs 79.4; MMLU 68.5 vs 69.6; GPQA 32.7 vs 34.6.
  quote: "Meta Agent Search (Empty Initialization) 73.9 ± 0.9 67.5 ± 3.3 68 .5 ± 3.3 32 .7 ± 3.2"
  where: App I, Table 6, p34. The explanation for math ("encouraged a broader and more diverse exploration") is a hypothesis.
- Cost of one search run.
  number: about $500 for ARC, about $300 for each Sec 4.2 domain, in OpenAI API costs.
  quote: "A single run of search and evaluation on ARC (Section 4.1) costs approximately $500 USD in OpenAI API costs, while a run within the reasoning and problem-solving domains (Section 4.2) costs about $300 USD."
  where: App J, p34. Most of the cost is evaluating discovered agents on gpt-3.5-turbo-0125.
- The loop mechanics (Algorithm 1, Sec 3, App B).
  number: archive seeded with baselines; 2 self-reflection rounds for novelty and correctness; up to 5 debug retries on runtime error; framework under 100 lines.
  quote: "If errors occur during evaluation, the meta agent performs a self-reflection step to refine the design, repeating this process up to five times if necessary."
  where: Sec 3, p4-5; App H, p33
  The metric the meta agent maximises is the validation score of each agent (success rate or F1). "Interestingness" is a prompt instruction, not a computed objective.
- Model-specific design: the best agent for GPT-3.5 used heavy multi-expert feedback, but on stronger models the agent with simpler feedback and more refinement did better.
  quote: "GPT-3.5 may have a worse capability in evaluating and refining the answers, so it needs a complex feedback mechanism for better refinement, while other advanced models benefit more from a simpler feedback mechanism."
  where: Sec 6, p10-11. This is interpretation, not an ablation.

LIMITS
- Only single-step QA tasks were tested. The authors say: "Currently, we only evaluate Meta Agent Search on single-step QA tasks".
- Evaluation is one scalar from running agents on a small validation set (20 questions for ARC, 128 for others, 32 for GPQA). The authors call it "both expensive and misses a lot of information" and suggest letting the meta agent read run logs.
- The search algorithm is simple: only "interestingness" is encouraged, with no quality-diversity or explore/exploit scheme.
- The meta agent is fixed (GPT-4 / gpt-4o). Higher-order ADAS, where the meta agent is itself improved, is future work.
- Single objective only (accuracy). Cost, latency and robustness are not optimised.
- All models are 2024-vintage (GPT-3.5, gpt-4o, Claude 3 Haiku, 3.5 Sonnet), and the baselines are those 2024 agent patterns. The ARC subset is tiny and easy.
- Safety: generated code ran in containers and was manually inspected. The authors concede model-generated code "could still act destructively". The paper does not test safety.
- Hand-designed baselines were reimplemented in the authors' own framework. Only a single search run per domain is reported, with no variance across search runs. The CIs cover evaluation sampling only.
- Test sets are separate from the validation sets used for search, but the paper has no check for the meta agent overfitting to validation. Cross-domain transfer is the only generalisation evidence.

BUILDS ON: Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022); Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2024) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023); COT-SC (Wang et al., 2023b); LLM Debate (Du et al., 2023); Intelligent Go-Explore / Quality-Diversity (Lu et al., 2024c); Step-back (Zheng et al., 2023); Role Assignment (Xu et al., 2023); OPRO (Yang et al., 2024) and PromptBreeder (Fernando et al., 2024) as prompt-only ADAS; FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) for the "forward" function framing; AI-GAs and AutoML (Clune, 2019; Hutter et al., 2019); Neural Architecture Search (Elsken et al., 2019); open-endedness and stepping stones (Lehman & Stanley, 2011; Wang et al., 2019); Meyerson et al. (2023) for LLM crossover; GPT-Swarm (Zhuge et al., 2024), DyLAN (Liu et al., 2023), DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) as graph/workflow search; AI Scientist, DiscoPOP, OMNI-EPIC (Lu et al., 2024b; Lu et al., 2024a; Faldor et al., 2024).

CODE
- Framework Info tuple (App C, Code 1, p23): `Info = namedtuple('Info', ['name', 'author', 'content', 'iteration_idx'])`
- Agent interface (App C, Code 1, p24-25): `class AgentSystem: def forward(self, taskInfo) -> Union[Info, str]:`
- Self-Reflection written as a "forward" function (App C, Code 2, p25). Loop shape: `for i in range(N_max): feedback, correct = critic_module([taskInfo, thinking, answer], critic_instruction, i); if correct.content == 'True': break; cot_inputs.extend([thinking, answer, feedback]); thinking, answer = cot_module(cot_inputs, cot_reflect_instruction, i + 1)`
- Meta-agent output contract (App B, p21): JSON with keys "thought", "name", "code", where "code" is `def forward(self, taskInfo):`.
- Pseudocode (App H, p33): for i in 1..N: design (reasoning, code, two self-reflections), evaluate on validation (refine up to 5 times on error), add to archive A; return A.
- Reflection prompt checklist (App B, p22): "1. Interestingness ... 2. Implementation Mistakes ... 3. Improvement".

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): the Meta Agent Search loop (meta agent, archive, test performance, refine until novel and error-free) plus three example discovered agents. This is the quickest one-picture explanation of the loop.
- Fig 2 (p3): the three ADAS components: search space, search algorithm, evaluation function.
- Fig 3 (p5): (a) held-out ARC accuracy per iteration, with annotated breakthroughs. This shows the archive and stepping-stone effect. (b) The best discovered agent's structure.
- Fig 4 (p26): an ARC task example. Low value for the note.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean overall. Table column alignment is flattened, so I re-read each row against its header. No embedded instructions found. The figure captions tool gave 4 captions (Figs 1-4). Fig 3a's exact accuracy values are not in the text and would need the image. Sec 4.1 says GPT-4 for the meta agent while the appendix names gpt-4o-2024-05-13, and Table 3 labels the gpt-4o column "GPT-4". I did not read the appendix G listings in full. The 13-14% best-agent ARC figure comes from Table 3 (13.7 ± 3.9 and 13.3 ± 3.8), not from the Fig 3a text.
